## Instructions

This is the template document for mini-project 3. You must use the template document for your code, since it will make it much easier to follow.

## Libraries and data load

Put whatever libraries you use here.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(glmnet)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ranger) # for random forests
```

Load your data here

```{r}
# Full Dataset
FullData_2025 <- read.csv("Data/FullData_2025.csv")
```

```{r}
# Clean Data [Helpful for graphs and Models]
FullData_2025 <- FullData_2025|>
  drop_na()

# Establish Factors 
FullData_2025<-FullData_2025|>
  mutate(Democracy=as.factor(Democracy), UN_member=as.factor(UN_member), world_4region=as.factor(world_4region))

head(FullData_2025)

```

**NOTE REGARDING DATA:** Please note that the data for each variable was collected from the last year provided in their respective datasets. For our purposes, we will be treated all variables as being collected from the year 2025 regardless of their most recent data. Below are the *actual* years each column was collected from:

*Democracy:* 2020

*CO2 Emissions:* 2022

*GDP per Capita:* 2025

*Human Development Index:* 2023

*People in Poverty:* 2025

*Gapminder Regions:* 2025

# Section 1: Oyinda

## Exploratory data analysis

For this section graph and find statistics for each of your 5 new predictor variables vs the response. You do not need to look at the predictor variables individually, although you can if you are considering logging.

## Variable 1: Democracy

### Graph and description

```{r}
#PLOT
FullData_2025 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Democracy, y = LifeExp)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Is the country a democracy?",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       title = "Life Expectancy in 2025 by Democracy Status")
```

From the boxplot, we can see that democracies tend to live longer than non-democracies. The median life expectancy is about 79 years for democracies and about 70 years for non-democracies. That is a gap of roughly 9 years. The middle halves of the two groups dont overlap. Non-democracies are more spread out, from about 55 to 81 years. Four democracies are outliers, with life expectancy of about 59 to 67 years.Democracy status looks like a useful predictor, but it does not directly prove that democracy causes longer life.Non-democracies are more spread out. Four democracies are low outliers: Lesotho, Ghana, Papua New Guinea, and Namibia.

### Stats and description

```{r}
Democracy_LifeExp_summary <- FullData_2025 |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarize(avg_lifeexp = mean(LifeExp),
            sd_lifeexp = sd(LifeExp),
            min_lifeexp = min(LifeExp),
            max_lifeexp = max(LifeExp),
            mdn_lifeexp = median(LifeExp),
            iqr_lifeexp = IQR(LifeExp),
            count = n())

Democracy_LifeExp_summary
FullData_2025 |>
  filter(Democracy == "Yes") |>
  slice_min(LifeExp, n = 4) |>
  select(name, LifeExp)

```

Democracies have a higher mean life expectancy than non-democracies, at 78.22 and 69.89 years. The medians are 79.00 and 70.39 years. Non-democracies vary more, with an SD of 6.31 and an IQR of 10.1, compared to 5.36 and 5.9 for democracies. The groups are about the same size, with 71 non-democracies and 69 democracies. The lowest democracy is Lesotho, at 58.71 years. Democracy looks like a strong predictor, because the gap is bigger than the spread within each group.

## Variable 2: *Number of Traffic Deaths Per 100k People*

### Graph and description

```{r}
FullData_2025 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Traffic_Deaths, y = LifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Traffic deaths per 100,000 people (log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       title = "Life Expectancy in 2025 vs. Traffic Deaths")

```

Countries with more traffic deaths tend to have lower life expectancy. The pattern is negative and slightly curved. Most countries have fewer than 40 deaths per 100,000 people. The points spread out more on the right side. Three countries are far to the right, at about 64, 76, and 96 deaths.Three countries are far to the right: Congo, Dem. Rep., Rwanda, and Uganda.

### Stats and description

```{r}
TrafficDeaths_summary <- FullData_2025 |>
  summarize(avg_td = mean(Traffic_Deaths),
            sd_td = sd(Traffic_Deaths),
            min_td = min(Traffic_Deaths),
            max_td = max(Traffic_Deaths),
            mdn_td = median(Traffic_Deaths),
            iqr_td = IQR(Traffic_Deaths),
            count = n())

TrafficDeaths_summary
FullData_2025 |>
  summarize(r = cor(Traffic_Deaths, LifeExp),
            r_log = cor(log10(Traffic_Deaths), LifeExp))
FullData_2025 |>
  slice_max(Traffic_Deaths, n = 3) |>
  select(name, Traffic_Deaths, LifeExp)
```

Traffic deaths range from 1.56 to 96.3 per 100,000 people across 140 countries. The mean is 18.13 and the median is 14.40, so a few high values pull the mean up. The SD is 16.03 and the IQR is 19.12. The correlation with life expectancy is -0.78, which is a strong negative relationship. The highest rates are in Congo, Dem. Rep. (96.30), Rwanda (76.42), and Uganda (63.70). I will log this variable, because the correlation improves to -0.83 after logging.

## Which variable for logging?

From your exploratory data analysis, which variable will need logged/did you log already ? Why?

Traffic deaths is the variable I will log. The data is skewed right. The mean (18.13) is higher than the median (14.40). A few African countries sit far out, with Congo, Dem. Rep. at 96.30 and Rwanda at 76.42 deaths per 100,000. Logging improves the correlation with life expectancy from -0.78 to -0.83. That means the relationship is closer to a straight line after logging.

## Logging predictor variables and splitting data

Split your data into an 80/20 training testing split after logging any variables that need logged.

```{r}
library(tidymodels)

# Log the variable that needs it
FullData_2025 <- FullData_2025 |>
  mutate(log_Traffic_Deaths = log10(Traffic_Deaths))

# Split the data 80/20
set.seed(1885)   # use the seed your assignment gives you
data_split <- initial_split(FullData_2025, prop = 0.80)

train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data  <- testing(data_split)
nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)

# Create list of only predictor variables
predictors <- c("Democracy", colnames(FullData_2025)[5:9],colnames(FullData_2025)[11:14])
```

# Section 2: Mia

## Lasso regression

### Making model

Make a lasso regression model for your response vs all predictors on the training data.

```{r}
FullData_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 10)

lasso_recipe <- recipe(as.formula(
  paste("LifeExp ~", 
        paste(predictors, collapse = " + "))), data = train_data) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> 
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

lasso_spec <- linear_reg(
  penalty = tune(),
  mixture = 1 #this is choosing LASSO
) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

lasso_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(lasso_recipe) |>
  add_model(lasso_spec)

lasso_tuned <- tune_grid(
  lasso_workflow,
  resamples = FullData_folds,
  grid = 50,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq, mae)
)
```

### Which variables

By looking at the slopes, which variables should be considered included in the model

```{r}
autoplot(lasso_tuned)
lasso_best <- select_best(lasso_tuned, metric = "rmse")
lasso_best
lasso_final_workflow <- finalize_workflow(lasso_workflow, lasso_best)
lasso_fit <- fit(lasso_final_workflow, data = train_data)
tidy(lasso_fit)
```

Based on the LASSO regression model, the variables to be considered include: HDI, log_Traffic_Deaths, and Sanitation.

*Note about `HDI`:* The use of HDI as a predictor for the `Life Expectancy` response variable should be approached with caution. Although the Human Development Index is the best performing variable according to the above graph, there is some overlap with the response variable because one of the measures of HDI accounts for life expectancy. This doesn't necessarily mean it can't be used in the model, but we should be aware of the direct relationship of these variables.

### Model evaluation-regression metrics on testing.

```{r}
regression_metrics <- metric_set(mse, rmse, mae)

lasso_test_results <- predict(lasso_fit, test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data |> select(LifeExp)) |>
  regression_metrics(truth = LifeExp, estimate = .pred)
lasso_test_results
```

## Regression Tree

### Making model

Make a regression tree model for your response vs all predictors on the training data.

```{r}
tree_spec <- decision_tree() |>
  set_mode("regression")|>
  set_engine("rpart", model=TRUE) 

tree_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(lasso_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)

LifeExp_tree=tree_workflow |>
  fit(data = train_data)

tree_object=LifeExp_tree |>
  extract_fit_engine() 
```

### Which variables

By looking at the tree, which variables should be considered included in the model

```{r}
rpart.plot(tree_object)
```

Based on the regression tree, the variables to consider include Sanitation, CO2, and HDI.

*Note about `HDI`:* The use of HDI as a predictor for the `Life Expectancy` response variable should be approached with caution. Although the Human Development Index is the best performing variable according to the above graph, there is some overlap with the response variable because one of the measures of HDI accounts for life expectancy. This doesn't necessarily mean it can't be used in the model, but we should be aware of the direct relationship of these variables.

### Model evaluation-regression metrics on testing

```{r}
LifeExp_tree_predict <- 
  tree_workflow |> 
  fit(data = test_data)

test_results <- augment(LifeExp_tree_predict, new_data = test_data)

test_results|>
  regression_metrics(truth = LifeExp, estimate = .pred)
```

# Section 3: Grace

## Random forest

### Making model

Make a random forest model for your response vs all predictors on the training data.

```{r}
LifExp_recipe=recipe(as.formula(
  paste("LifeExp ~", 
        paste(predictors, collapse = " + "))),
  data=train_data) # only count 10 predictor variables

tree_spec <- rand_forest() |>
  set_mode("regression")|>
  set_engine("ranger",importance = "impurity") #Impurity here is sum of squares residual

rf_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(LifExp_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)

LifeExp_rf=rf_workflow |>
  fit(data = train_data) 
```

### Which variables

By looking at the variable importance plot, which variables should be considered included in the model

```{r}
importance_values <- LifeExp_rf |>
  extract_fit_engine() |> 
  ranger::importance() 

importance_df=importance_values <- tibble(
  Variable = names(importance_values),
  Importance = importance_values
)

importance_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance), y = Importance)) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_flip() +  # Makes variables easy to read vertically
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest Variable Importance",
    x = "Features",
    y = "Importance (Impurity reduction)"
  )
```

From the graph, the main variables that we would consider to include in the model are `HDI` and `Sanitation` since they had the highest importance according to the results of the graph. Other variables that could also be considered are `Internet Users`and `Traffic Deaths` followed by `GDP`.

*Note about `HDI`:* The use of HDI as a predictor for the `Life Expectancy` response variable should be approached with caution. Although the Human Development Index is the best performing variable according to the above graph, there is some overlap with the response variable because one of the measures of HDI accounts for life expectancy. This doesn't necessarily mean it can't be used in the model, but we should be aware of the direct relationship of these variables.

### Model evaluation-regression metrics on testing.

```{r}
regression_metrics <- metric_set(mse, rmse, mae)

LifeExp_rf_predict <- 
  rf_workflow |> 
  fit(data = test_data)

test_results <- augment(LifeExp_rf_predict, new_data = test_data) ## adding original data


rf_regress_test=test_results|>
  regression_metrics(truth = LifeExp, estimate = .pred)
rf_regress_test
```

## Variable selection comparison

What were the similarities and the difference between the variables selected for each model.

Overall, across all three models, HDI and Sanitation were determined as the primary predictors of Life Expectancy, consistently ranking as the top two. Looking beyond the top two, the models diverged in their choices. LASSO prioritized log_Traffic_Deaths, the Decision Tree prioritized CO2, and the Random Forest prioritized Internet users as third place predictors. Despise the differences in the third best predictor variable, log_Traffic_Deaths was still a strong consideration in two models, LASSO and Random Forest (coming in 4th place after Internet users). The Decision Tree's exclusion of a fourth predictor variable makes it unable to determine if log_Traffic_Deaths was also considered.

## Best model

Which model would you recommend your team use? Why? Are there trade-offs between interpretability and model metrics?

The recommended model to use would be the Random Forest model. This was chosen as the recommended model because it had the lowest set of evaludation metrics on the test data across all the models created in this document. The trade-off is that the result of creating the Random Forest model does not indicate by how much the best predictor variables influence the response Life Expectancy. The result only shows the graph that plots the importance, not the impact values. Although this trade-off exists, it is still the top choice based on the evaluating metrics on the test set.
